name: Rose Red
lede: Rose red is the red of a garden rose, a name naturalists fixed on a chart as a pale pink in the early 1800s and one that screens now show as a deep crimson-pink.

sections.title: Two rose reds
sections.body:
*Rose red* has meant a pale pink and a vivid crimson, sometimes in the same century. Paterson's dictionary gives it simply as a vivid red [7]. The chart where naturalists fixed the name defines it very differently, as carmine red lightened with plenty of snow white and a touch of cochineal red [1].

Our library holds both ends. The aged Werner swatch for rose red is a pale cream-pink, #EEDAC3, Ridgway's 1912 plate is a strong rose, #D1294E, and the swatch on this page, #C21E56, is deeper still [9]. Its nearest named neighbor today is [[raspberry]], with [[carmine]] and [[old-rose]] close by in the same part of the wheel [9]. This is a different color from [[rose-pink]], which is lighter and bluer [9].

sections.title: A rose on Syme's chart
sections.body:
In Patrick Syme's chart of reds, rose red is number 89, set between flesh red (88) and peach blossom red (90) [2]. Its natural example is the common garden rose, and its mineral is figure stone [2]. Syme defined [[flesh-red]] in turn as a blend of rose red, tile red and a touch of white, so the rose sits one step upstream of the skin tone [1].

Our library files the entry under Werner, because Syme's chart is Werner's revised [9]. Baty traces number 89 itself to the French system of Picardet, one of two reds in the 1821 edition taken from there, rather than to Werner's own reds [14][9]. Baty's modern illustrations for the entry are rose petals from Rössig's rose atlas and a flamingo's feathers [1].

Syme was not coining a new term. Rose-red appears in several of the eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century lists of color names that Baty tabulates [4]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930 gives about 1300 as its first record, a date we could not check against the underlying sources [9].

sections.title: How a rose red was made
sections.body:
An earlier recipe is almost the same as Syme's [3]. In 1769 Jacob Schäffer's chart of reds listed no. 71, rose red, as cochineal mixed with lead white [3]. His table had 150 numbered compartments, of which only 33 were painted, and the student was left to fill the rest by mixing [3]. Both recipes make the same point: a rose red of this period was a lake of cochineal or carmine thinned with white.

The name lives on in paints and ceramics. The *Pigment Compendium* records that Salter (1869) described a tin-chromium pigment that took on a rose-red color after an acid wash, which the Compendium treats as probably the same as mineral lake or potter's pink [15]. It also lists Thalo Red Rose as an American proprietary name for a quinacridone red [16].

sections.title: Rose red in writing and in the eye
sections.body:
Chevreul's observation, quoted by Jarman, is a lesson for the eye: placed beside even a rosy complexion, rose red and light crimson rob it of freshness and push it toward green [17]. It is simultaneous contrast at work, and it is easy to test with a red sleeve held beside a cheek.

Greenfield uses the word in two places. In a translation of Aztec accounts, women pray that their daughters will dye feathers in varied colors, rose red among them, and the Aztec word for red, *tlapalli*, also meant color in general [18]. Later she describes rose-red geraniums on her kitchen windowsill in a snowbound Massachusetts winter and imagines that this was all the red the world had [19]. Birren recalls Schubert comparing E minor to a maiden in white with a rose-red bow [20].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is one of the rarest colors in our archive of 23,781 paintings [10]. A color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only one work, [[painting:cma-164465|a large multi-armed figure of about 1900]], where it fills 29 per cent [10]. That makes it rarer than 86 per cent of the named colors [10]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color, not a pigment test [10].

In Google Books the phrase *rose red* peaked in the 1820s, the decade after Syme's second edition, and has been flatter since, though the count covers every sense of the words [11].

questions.q: Why does the swatch on this page differ from Syme's rose red?
choices: The word drifted from a pale pink toward a vivid red
The swatch was photographed from a faded chart
Syme's rose red was darker than crimson
Rose red is a different color on each screen by law
questions.answer: The word drifted from a pale pink toward a vivid red

In 1769 Schäffer made rose red from cochineal and lead white.
